opus-5.5.text:
I think pre-training is still very important, but the way we think about it has shifted. For a long time, scaling pre-training was the main lever: more compute, more data, bigger models, and you'd see fairly predictable gains across the board. With reasoning models, we now have a second axis. We can spend compute at training time through reinforcement learning, and at inference time by letting the model think longer.

These two aren't really in competition, though. Pre-training gives the model its base understanding of the world: its knowledge, its intuitions, its ability to model language and concepts. Reasoning builds on top of that. A model that thinks for a long time but starts from a weaker foundation will hit limits. It might explore a lot, but it won't have the right instincts about which directions are promising. So a stronger pre-trained model makes reasoning more efficient and more capable.

What has changed is the balance. We're now asking where the marginal unit of compute is best spent, and increasingly a lot of it goes to RL and to letting models work on harder problems over longer horizons. But I'd expect both to keep scaling together. The really exciting outcome isn't one replacing the other. It's what they unlock in combination: models that can actually carry out extended research, make novel discoveries, and work autonomously on problems for a long time. Getting there will take progress on both fronts.

r001.rationale: The response says stronger pre-training makes reasoning more efficient and capable, and expects both to keep scaling together, with their combination unlocking more ambitious work. This communicates compounding benefits.

fable-5.1.text:
I think pre-training remains really fundamental, and I'd push back a bit on the framing that reasoning somehow replaces it. The way I see it, pre-training is where the model acquires its world model. It's where it learns the structure of language, of code, of mathematics, of how the world works. Reasoning, and the reinforcement learning on top of it, is about learning how to use that knowledge effectively, how to think for longer, how to check your work, how to plan.

Those two things compound. If you have a stronger base model, every unit of reasoning compute you spend on top of it goes further, because the model is reasoning from better intuitions. And conversely, reasoning gives us a way to extract much more value from a given level of pre-training than we could before. So I don't think of it as scaling pre-training versus scaling reasoning. It's really two axes, and the frontier is defined by how you move along both.

What has changed is the economics. For a while, pre-training was essentially the only lever we had, so all the compute went there. Now we have a second lever with a steep return curve, and so the question becomes one of allocation. Where is the marginal dollar best spent? And that answer shifts over time. There are moments where the reasoning side has been the fastest-moving part, and I think that's gotten a lot of attention, but the base model is still the thing that determines the ceiling of what reasoning can reach.

I'd also say there's an interplay in the data. Reasoning models generate a lot of high-quality synthetic trajectories, and that feeds back into what you can pre-train on. So the boundary between the two stages is actually getting blurrier, not sharper.

The thing I'm most interested in is less about any specific technique and more about the trajectory. If you zoom out, we're seeing steady progress in the models' ability to do genuinely long, hard intellectual work. That's what matters for things like automating research. And getting there is going to require continued progress on both fronts, better foundations and better ways to think on top of them.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training and reasoning “compound,” explaining that a stronger base makes reasoning compute more effective and reasoning extracts more value from pre-training.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling pre-training remains very important. Reasoning gives us another way to improve models: we can train them to work through problems, and give them more time to do that at inference. But those capabilities build on the foundation established during pre-training.

So I see these as complementary directions. A stronger base model gives reasoning training a better starting point, and reasoning lets us get more out of that foundation. The interesting question is how to allocate compute across pre-training, post-training, and inference to get the greatest improvement. That balance can change without pre-training becoming unimportant.

r001.rationale: The response describes the directions as complementary: a stronger pre-trained base improves reasoning training, and reasoning gets more out of that foundation, communicating mutual benefits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling pre-training remains very important. Reasoning gives us another way to improve models—by letting them spend more computation working through a problem—but that computation builds on the capabilities learned during pre-training.

So I see these as complementary directions. A stronger base model can make better use of reasoning, and reasoning can help us get more out of that base model. The interesting question is how to balance compute across pre-training, post-training, and inference. That balance will evolve, but I don’t think progress in reasoning makes pre-training less fundamental.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training and reasoning as complementary, with a stronger base improving reasoning and reasoning extracting more from that base—communicating mutually reinforcing benefits.
